src.q: Each tablet contains 10 mg propranolol hydrochloride.

items.t: Hypertension; angina; long-term prevention of re-infarction after MI; most cardiac dysrhythmias; migraine prophylaxis; essential tremor; situational and generalised anxiety (somatic symptoms); prophylaxis of upper GI bleeding in portal hypertension with oesophageal varices; adjunct in thyrotoxicosis; hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; peri-operative phaeochromocytoma (with an alpha-blocker).

src.q: a) the control of hypertension; b) the management of angina pectoris; c) long term management against re-infarction after recovery from acute myocardial infarction; d) the control of most forms of cardiac dysrhythmias; e) the prophylaxis of migraine; f) the management of essential tremor;
h) prophylaxis of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in patients with portal hypertension and oesophageal varices;

restrictions.note: No prescribing restriction stated in the UK propranolol 10 mg tablets SmPC.

items.t: Hypertension: start 80 mg twice daily, increase weekly by response; usual 160-320 mg per day.

src.q: A starting dose of 80 mg twice a day may be increased at weekly intervals according to response. The usual dose range is 160 to 320 mg per day.

items.t: Angina, migraine, essential tremor: start 40 mg two or three times daily, increase weekly; usual 80-160 mg/day (migraine, tremor) or 120-240 mg/day (angina).

src.q: A starting dose of 40 mg two or three times daily may be increased by the same amount at weekly intervals according to patient response.
An adequate response in migraine and essential tremor is usually seen in the range 80 to 160 mg/day and in angina in the range 120 to 240 mg/day.

items.t: Anxiety: 40 mg daily for acute situational anxiety; generalised anxiety 40 mg twice daily, up to 40 mg three times daily. Review after 6-12 months.

src.q: A dose of 40 mg daily may provide short term relief of acute situational anxiety.
usually responds adequately to 40 mg twice daily which, in individual cases, may be increased to 40 mg three times daily.
Patients should be reviewed after 6 to 12 months treatment.

items.t: Arrhythmias, anxiety tachycardia, HOCM, thyrotoxicosis: 10-40 mg three or four times daily.

src.q: A dosage range of 10 to 40 mg three or four times a day usually achieves the required response.

items.t: Post-MI: start between day 5 and 21; 40 mg four times daily for 2-3 days, then 80 mg twice daily.

src.q: Treatment should start between days 5 and 21 after myocardial infarction, with an initial dose of 40 mg four times a day for 2 or 3 days.
the total daily dosage may thereafter be given as 80 mg twice a day.

items.t: Portal hypertension: start 40 mg twice daily, increase to 80 mg twice daily by heart rate (aim about 25% reduction); maximum 160 mg twice daily.

src.q: Dosage should begin with 40 mg twice daily, increasing to 80 mg twice daily depending on heart rate response. If necessary, the dose may be increased incrementally to a maximum of 160 mg twice daily.

items.t: Elderly: use with caution; start with the lowest dose.

src.q: Inderal should be used to treat the elderly with caution. It is suggested that treatment should start with the lowest dose.

items.t: Dysrhythmias, phaeochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis: 0.25-0.5 mg/kg three or four times daily as required (guide only).

src.q: Oral: 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg three or four times daily as required.

items.t: Migraine: under 12 years 20 mg two or three times daily; over 12 years adult dose.

src.q: Migraine Oral: Under the age of 12: 20 mg two or three times daily. Over the age of 12: The adult dose.

items.t: Fallot's tetralogy: up to 1 mg/kg three or four times daily as required (guide only).

src.q: Oral: Up to 1 mg/kg repeated three or four times daily as required.

items.t: Hypersensitivity to propranolol or any excipient.

src.q: Hypersensitivity to the active substance(s) or to any of the excipients listed in section 6.1.

items.t: History of bronchial asthma or bronchospasm.

src.q: Inderal must not be used if there is a history of bronchial asthma or bronchospasm.

items.t: Bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; hypotension; metabolic acidosis; after prolonged fasting; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; second- or third-degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; uncontrolled heart failure; Prinzmetal's angina.

src.q: as with other beta-blockers must not be used in patients with any of the following conditions:

bradycardia; cardiogenic shock; hypotension; metabolic acidosis; after prolonged fasting; severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances; second or third degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome; untreated phaeochromocytoma; uncontrolled heart failure or Prinzmetal's angina.

items.t: Patients prone to hypoglycaemia (e.g. after prolonged fasting, or with restricted counter-regulatory reserve: malnutrition, starvation, chronic liver disease, diabetes, drugs blocking catecholamine response).

src.q: Inderal must not be used in patients prone to hypoglycaemia, i.e., patients after prolonged fasting or patients with restricted counter-regulatory reserves.

Patients at risk for an inadequate response to hypoglycaemia includes individuals with malnutrition, prolonged fasting, starvation, chronic liver disease, diabetes and concomitant use of drugs which block the full response to catecholamines.

items.t: Controlled heart failure: may be used; caution with poor cardiac reserve. First-degree heart block: caution.

src.q: may be used in patients whose signs of heart failure have been controlled. Caution must be exercised in patients whose cardiac reserve is poor.
caution must be exercised if it is given to patients with first degree heart block.

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: may mask signs (tachycardia); can cause hypoglycaemia even in non-diabetics (neonates, children, elderly, haemodialysis, chronic liver disease, overdose), rarely with seizures or coma. Caution with hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetes.

src.q: Inderal occasionally causes hypoglycaemia, even in non-diabetic patients
Severe hypoglycaemia associated with Inderal has rarely presented with seizures and/or coma in isolated patients.
Caution must be exercised in the concurrent use of Inderal and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetic patients.

items.t: Do not stop abruptly: withdraw over 7-14 days, following patients (especially ischaemic heart disease). If stopping before surgery, stop at least 24 hours before.

src.q: Abrupt withdrawal of beta-blockers is to be avoided. The dosage should be withdrawn gradually over a period of 7 to 14 days.
this should be done at least 24 hours prior to the procedure.

items.t: Hepatic or renal impairment: half-life may increase; caution when starting and choosing the first dose. Decompensated cirrhosis: use with caution. Portal hypertension: liver function may worsen and hepatic encephalopathy may develop.

src.q: Since the half-life may be increased in patients with significant hepatic or renal impairment, caution must be exercised when starting treatment and selecting the initial dose.
Inderal must be used with caution in patients with decompensated cirrhosis
In patients with portal hypertension, liver function may deteriorate and hepatic encephalopathy may develop.

items.t: History of anaphylaxis: more severe reactions to allergens; may not respond to usual adrenaline doses.

src.q: may cause a more severe reaction to a variety of allergens when given to patients with a history of anaphylactic reaction to such allergens.

items.t: May aggravate less severe peripheral arterial disease; may mask thyrotoxicosis; in phaeochromocytoma use only with an alpha-blocker.

src.q: may also aggravate less severe peripheral arterial circulatory disturbances.
may mask the signs of thyrotoxicosis.
in patients with phaeochromocytoma, an alpha-blocker may be given concomitantly.

items.t: Galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption: should not take (contains lactose).

src.q: Patients with rare hereditary problems of galactose intolerance, total lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption should not take this medicine.

items.t: Verapamil or diltiazem: should not be combined; exaggerated negative inotropic and conduction effects can cause severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure. Do not give either IV within 48 hours of stopping the other.

src.q: should not be used in combination with calcium channel blockers with negative inotropic effects (e.g. verapamil, diltiazem)
This may result in severe hypotension, bradycardia and cardiac failure.

items.t: Dihydropyridines (e.g. nifedipine): more risk of hypotension; cardiac failure with latent cardiac insufficiency; blood levels of either may change, so dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: Concomitant therapy with dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, e.g., nifedipine, may increase the risk of hypotension, and cardiac failure may occur in patients with latent cardiac insufficiency.

items.t: Insulin and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetes: caution; tachycardia of hypoglycaemia is masked and the hypoglycaemic response to insulin may be prolonged.

src.q: Caution must be exercised in the concurrent use of Inderal and hypoglycaemic therapy in diabetic patients. Inderal may prolong the hypoglycaemic response to insulin

items.t: Warfarin, theophylline, rifampicin, quinidine, propafenone, thioridazine, dihydropyridines: hepatic enzyme interactions; blood levels of either medicine may change, so dose adjustment may be needed.

src.q: quinidine, propafenone, rifampicin, theophylline, warfarin, thioridazine and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers
Owing to the fact that blood concentrations of either agent may be affected, dosage adjustments may be needed according to clinical judgement

items.t: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen): may reduce the blood pressure lowering effect.

src.q: Concomitant use of prostaglandin synthetase inhibiting drugs eg, ibuprofen and indometacin, may decrease the hypotensive effects of Inderal.

items.t: IV lidocaine infusion: lidocaine levels rise about 30%; avoid the combination.

src.q: Administration of Inderal during infusion of lidocaine may increase the plasma concentration of lidocaine by approximately 30%.
The combination should be avoided.

items.t: Rizatriptan: exposure rises 70-80%; use rizatriptan 5 mg. Adrenaline/sympathomimetics: may counteract beta-blockade; caution with parenteral adrenaline. Clonidine: withdraw the beta-blocker several days before clonidine. Ergotamine: caution (vasospasm). Cimetidine, hydralazine and alcohol raise propranolol levels. Chlorpromazine: levels of both rise.

src.q: If both drugs are to be used, a rizatriptan dose of 5 mg has been recommended.
Concomitant use of sympathomimetic agents e.g., adrenaline, may counteract the effect of beta-blockers.
Concomitant use of cimetidine or hydralazine will increase plasma levels of propranolol

items.t: Significant renal impairment: half-life may be longer; use caution when starting and choosing the initial dose.

src.q: Since the half-life may be increased in patients with significant hepatic or renal impairment, caution must be exercised when starting treatment and selecting the initial dose.

items.t: Significant hepatic impairment: half-life may be longer; caution when starting and choosing the initial dose.

items.t: Decompensated cirrhosis: use with caution; may increase the risk of hepatic encephalopathy in portal hypertension.

src.q: Inderal must be used with caution in patients with decompensated cirrhosis
There have been reports suggesting that treatment with propranolol may increase the risk of developing hepatic encephalopathy

items.t: SmPC: should not be given in pregnancy unless essential. Not teratogenic, but beta-blockers reduce placental perfusion (fetal death, premature delivery); neonatal hypoglycaemia and bradycardia may occur.

src.q: As with all drugs Inderal should not be given during pregnancy unless its use is essential.
However beta-blockers reduce placental perfusion, which may result in intra-uterine foetal death, immature and premature deliveries.
In addition, adverse effects (especially hypoglycaemia and bradycardia in the neonate and bradycardia in the foetus) may occur.

items.t: BUMPS: can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor; no concerns that it causes harm; extra growth scans may be offered.

src.q: Propranolol can be used in pregnancy if recommended by a doctor.
There are no concerns that taking propranolol in pregnancy causes harm.
you may be offered additional scans at around 32 and 36 weeks

items.t: SmPC: beta-blockers pass into breast milk; breastfeeding is not recommended.

src.q: Breast-feeding is therefore not recommended following administration of these compounds.

items.t: SPS: a beta-blocker of choice in breastfeeding (very small amounts in milk); as a precaution monitor the infant for bradycardia or hypoglycaemia.

src.q: Propranolol is a preferred choice due to very small amounts in breast milk and favourable pharmacokinetics although monitoring is still recommended.

reproductive.note: No fertility or contraception advice in the UK propranolol 10 mg tablets SmPC. BUMPS: no increased risk expected if the father took propranolol.

items.t: Rare: bronchospasm in asthma (sometimes fatal), worsening heart failure, heart block, postural hypotension with syncope, thrombocytopenia. Hypoglycaemia (not known) with seizures in at-risk groups.

src.q: Rare Bronchospasm may occur in patients with bronchial asthma or a history of asthmatic complaints, sometimes with fatal outcome
Rare Heart failure deterioration, precipitation of heart block, postural hypotension, which may be associated with syncope
Rare Thrombocytopaenia

items.t: Overdose: severe toxicity (bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmias, seizures, coma). Tell patients the signs and to seek urgent help after an overdose.

src.q: Propranolol is known to cause severe toxicity when used in overdose.
Patients should be informed of the signs of overdose and advised to seek urgent medical assistance if an overdose of propranolol has been taken.
